summaries.example: Imagine looking at a fast-spinning colored stick. It may seem to make a circle, even though the stick is straight. Auriol used examples like this to ask whether seeing is simply copying the world. He thought the senses actively make an object appear to us in a special way.
summaries.summary: Peter Auriol was a French Franciscan teacher and philosopher who lived around 1280–1322. Most of his surviving writing is about theology, but it also explores many philosophical questions. He studied earlier thinkers closely, then built his own connected system of ideas. Auriol held that only individual things exist outside the mind. For example, particular people and trees are real; the general idea “person” is made by the mind from such individuals. He also said that sensing and thinking are active processes. A thing becomes present to a knower as esse apparens, or apparent being: the thing as it appears through a sense or thought. This helped him explain mistakes in perception, such as a stick looking bent in water. Auriol also argued that God knows the future in a special way that does not remove human free will. He proposed that some statements about future events are not yet simply true or false. His ideas about categories, being, knowledge, and freedom influenced later medieval debates.
key_ideas: Auriol carefully studied earlier thinkers and often offered unusual answers to their disagreements.
He said that individual things are real outside the mind, while general ideas are formed by the mind.
He thought seeing and thinking are active: our senses and intellect make things appear to us.
He tried to protect human free will while also discussing God’s knowledge and judgment.
He distinguished direct-looking knowledge from knowledge built through imagination or reasoning.
summaries.why_it_matters: Auriol’s questions are still recognizable. We often ask whether our ideas show the world as it is, how mistakes happen, and whether people can be responsible for choices. His work also shows that philosophy grows through careful disagreement: he learned from earlier thinkers, challenged them, and gave later thinkers new problems to consider.

A view that only individual things, such as one person or one tree, exist outside the mind; general ideas are made by thinking.

summaries.example: Suppose an astronomer calculates that an eclipse will occur and imagines it from the calculation. This is not the same as directly seeing an eclipse. For Auriol, intuitive cognition has the character of directness and apparent presence, while abstractive cognition is mediated and discursive. Yet an appearance can seem present even when its object is absent, as in an afterimage or illusion. Therefore, the distinction depends on how cognition appears, not simply on whether the object exists or is physically present.
summaries.summary: Peter Auriol, a French Franciscan active in the early fourteenth century, developed a highly systematic and historically engaged philosophy within predominantly theological works. He often opposed or revised positions associated with Aquinas, Henry of Ghent, and Duns Scotus. In metaphysics, he treated only five Aristotelian categories as existing extra-mentally and regarded the others as dependent on conceptual activity. He also described being as an indeterminate concept that includes all beings without requiring an external differentiating addition. Auriol’s conceptualism maintains that only singulars exist in reality outside the mind. Individual things possess non-universal essential aspects, or rationes, whose maximal similarity across individuals explains how the intellect forms shared universal concepts. His account of cognition centers on esse apparens. In sensing or understanding, a cognitive power puts the object into a mode of being as perceived or conceived; the object is not replaced by an independently existing mental representation. Illusions therefore reveal a general activity present in both mistaken and accurate cognition. Auriol’s theory of intuitive and abstractive cognition is phenomenological: the distinction concerns whether cognition appears direct, present, and actualizing, or mediated and discursive, rather than depending simply on the object’s actual presence. He denies that people in this life experience intuitive intellectual cognition, which limits the reach of unaided human reason. In debates about future contingents, he tried to preserve both divine knowledge and human freedom by saying that God knows future events without knowing them as future, and by allowing future-tensed propositions a neutral status. key_ideas: Auriol’s thought is systematic: recurring principles connect his accounts of categories, being, cognition, and freedom.
He accepted a univocal concept of being but treated it as indeterminate, containing other concepts implicitly rather than receiving an outside differentiating feature.
Of Aristotle’s ten categories, he treated substance, quality, quantity, action, and passion as extra-mental; he treated relation, place, time, position, and state or habit as conceptual.
His conceptualism identifies concepts with particulars in esse apparens, while using similar individual rationes to explain why one universal concept can apply to many things.
Because perceptual error reveals that cognition actively produces appearances, Auriol must explain reliable perception rather than merely explaining error.
Auriol held that intuitive and abstractive cognition differ by their mode of appearance, and that humans in this life do not experience intuitive intellectual cognition.
summaries.why_it_matters: Auriol matters because he links questions usually treated separately: what exists, how concepts refer, why perception can err, what human beings can know, and whether freedom survives divine foreknowledge. His positions also illustrate how medieval philosophers used detailed criticism of predecessors to construct new theories. The later responses to Auriol show that a theory can be influential even when other thinkers reject its conclusions.

important_terms.definition: The view that only singular individuals have real, extra-mental existence; universals are produced by intellectual cognition but have a basis in individual things.
A special mode of existence in which an object is present as cognized or perceived. It is not a separate mental copy with its own independent real being.
An individual thing’s non-universal essential aspect, which can guide the intellect toward forming a concept.
A universal, general concept that can apply to many individuals, although Auriol grounds it in maximally similar aspects of those individuals.
A concept or term whose primary meaning also brings along a secondary meaning, such as “flesh,” which suggests the living thing to which it belongs.
Cognition characterized by directness, apparent presentness, and the appearance that its object is actual or existing.
Cognition reached mediately or through a discursive process; for Auriol, ordinary human intellectual cognition in this life is abstractive.
The philosophical problem of how God’s knowledge of future events can coexist with genuinely open human choice.

If future-tense propositions are neither true nor false, what kind of knowledge can a statement about a future event provide?
Can a theory that begins with perceptual error adequately explain reliable perception?
Why might rejecting intuitive intellectual cognition limit what unaided human reason can prove?
Does Auriol’s account of free will answer the problem of divine immutability, or relocate it to the nature of divine knowledge?

summaries.example: Think about a straw in a glass of water. It can look bent even though it is straight. Auriol would say the sense of sight does not merely receive a perfect picture. It actively presents the straw in a certain way. In a normal case, how the object appears matches the object outside the mind. In an illusion, the appearance and the outside object do not match. This difference helped Auriol explain why mistakes are possible without saying that all seeing is unreliable.
summaries.summary: Peter Auriol was a French Franciscan philosopher and theologian who lived in the late thirteenth and early fourteenth centuries. He wrote mainly as a teacher of theology, but his work explored many philosophical problems. His method was to examine earlier thinkers, identify difficulties in their views, and propose a tightly connected alternative. Auriol’s conceptualism says that only individual things—this person, that horse, or one particular tree—exist outside the mind. General ideas, or universals, are formed by the intellect. Still, these ideas are not disconnected from reality. Individual things contain essential aspects, called rationes, and similar aspects in different individuals guide the mind toward similar concepts. Auriol’s theory of esse apparens explains how cognition works. When the senses or intellect know something, they make it appear in a special mode. This is not a separate object floating inside the mind; it is the object as sensed or understood. Optical illusions show why an appearance may fail to match extra-mental reality. Auriol therefore gives error an important role in explaining cognition, while maintaining that our natural faculties usually work reliably. He also distinguished intuitive cognition, which appears direct and present, from abstractive cognition, which is mediated or discursive. Unlike Duns Scotus, he did not make the distinction depend simply on whether the object exists or is present. In questions about the future, Auriol held both that God knows future events and that human beings have free will. He proposed that God knows the future in a way that does not turn human actions into necessities, and he used a logic in which some future claims are neither true nor false yet. key_ideas: Auriol was a medieval Franciscan thinker whose work joined theology with metaphysics, logic, and the study of the mind.
He argued that only individual things exist outside the mind, but that general concepts can still be based on real features of individuals.
His theory of esse apparens says that sensing and thinking actively make objects appear to us.
Auriol used illusions to show that appearances do not always match reality, while still treating ordinary cognition as generally dependable.
He disagreed with Duns Scotus about intuitive and abstractive cognition: the difference depends on how cognition appears, not only on whether its object is present.
He tried to explain divine foreknowledge and predestination in a way that left room for human choice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Auriol’s philosophy matters because it asks how minds connect with the world. Those questions appear in modern discussions of perception, concepts, uncertainty, and responsibility. His work also reminds us that a historical philosopher can be important not because everyone accepted the view, but because the view changed the questions later thinkers had to answer.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical view that individual things are real outside the mind, while general ideas are made by the mind from those individuals.
A thing as it exists for a knower when it is sensed or understood; Auriol did not treat this as a separate copy of the thing.
A general idea that can apply to many individual things, such as the idea “tree” applying to many trees.
A particular thing’s essential aspect that can guide the mind in forming a concept.
The power to make choices; Auriol treated human free will as a basic starting point in his account of the future.
Knowledge that seems direct and present, like seeing something before you.
Knowledge reached indirectly, through imagining, thinking, or a chain of reasoning.

questions_to_think_about: If universals exist only in the mind, how can science make claims about many things?
